title: IndiGo Leans on Mumbai and Premium Cabins as Pakistan Airspace Closure Disrupts Westward Flights
excerpt: With Delhi's westward routes squeezed by the closure of Pakistani airspace and jet fuel prices elevated, IndiGo CEO Willie Walsh says the airline will push European growth through Mumbai, keep its Amsterdam slots with the A321XLR, and go premium on the A350 from 2028.
body:
• The closure of Pakistani airspace has hit IndiGo's westward flying from Delhi hardest, CEO Willie Walsh said on November 2, while Mumbai offers room to add European destinations with the A321XLR.
  • IndiGo has 60 Airbus A350s on order, with the first due in the second quarter of 2028; the first 10 will carry 16 lie-flat business seats plus premium economy and economy.
  • The airline will keep flying the A321XLR to Amsterdam to retain its airport slots until the A350s arrive, and its XLR fleet grows from four aircraft to seven next year.
  • For India-Europe travellers, the practical effect is a network tilting toward Mumbai and Navi Mumbai, with a proper lie-flat premium cabin only from 2028 — check routings carefully before booking westward trips this winter.

India's largest airline is redrawing its long-haul map around a closed sky. Speaking at a media briefing in New Delhi on Monday, November 2, IndiGo Chief Executive Officer Willie Walsh said the closure of Pakistani airspace affected Delhi, while Mumbai offered opportunities to serve additional European destinations with the A321XLR, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. Reuters reported the same briefing as IndiGo considering fast-tracking parts of its overseas growth because westward flights are disrupted.

Why westward flying got harder

Three pressures have converged on IndiGo's long-haul operation. First, the Pakistani airspace restrictions force longer routings on westbound departures from northern India, which is why Delhi is the most exposed hub. Second, the crisis in West Asia, along with other global events, has pushed up jet fuel prices, Walsh said. Third, IndiGo competes on those routes against carriers with substantial fuel-price protection: Walsh said major Asian carriers were typically around 40 per cent hedged, while European airlines were generally around 70 to 80 per cent hedged. He said that difference had complicated competition during IndiGo's leased Boeing 787 operations, alongside the airspace restrictions and elevated fuel costs. IndiGo has since discontinued the damp-leased Boeing 787-9 long-haul services.

IndiGo is reviewing its fuel-hedging policy in response, but has not decided to start hedging. Walsh said the issue was discussed with the board last week and management would return after a more comprehensive assessment. Remaining unhedged was currently the right approach, he said, and hedging while domestic competitors remained unhedged could itself introduce competitive risk.

"Our long-haul expansion gives us an opportunity to review our hedging policy."

— Willie Walsh, Chief Executive Officer, IndiGo

The workaround: Mumbai, the XLR, and Amsterdam slots

The near-term growth engine is the single-aisle A321XLR. IndiGo has four in operation, with the fleet expected to increase to seven next year. Walsh said IndiGo would continue operating A321XLR services to Amsterdam to retain airport slots until the arrival of the A350 fleet — a detail that matters for travellers, because it keeps a nonstop India-Amsterdam link alive through the transition. Amsterdam is a route IndiGo knows well: it launched its long-haul debut there from Mumbai in July 2025, a service the airline still showcases in its official press release on goindigo.in.

Walsh identified Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru as the cities from which IndiGo would look at international services, and described Navi Mumbai airport as a significant long-term opportunity, with IndiGo planning to expand across both Mumbai airports. He maintained that long-term expansion plans remain unchanged, and that the existing domestic network — IndiGo holds around 65 per cent of India's domestic market — could feed long-haul services without redesigning the short-haul operation.

Going premium on the A350

The bigger shift lands in 2028. The first A350-900 aircraft are expected to join the fleet in the second quarter of 2028, subject to Airbus and supplier readiness, Walsh told reporters. IndiGo has 60 A350s on order. The configuration for the first 10 has been finalized: 16 lie-flat seats in business class, alongside premium economy and economy cabins — a three-class layout from an airline built on a no-frills model. The airline is debating whether to increase the number of business-class seats in subsequent deliveries, and Walsh said he personally believed there was a strong case for doing so. He also said IndiGo would continue investing in its Stretch offering, and that cargo would be a critical component of future long-haul operations after encouraging performance during the leased wide-body programme.

What it means for travellers

For the diaspora reader flying between India and Europe, the immediate takeaway is routing, not cabins. Westward departures from Delhi face the airspace detour; Mumbai-origin services are where IndiGo sees growth room now. The premium product — a lie-flat seat on an IndiGo wide-body — does not arrive until the A350s enter service in 2028, so anyone booking for this winter is choosing among the current XLR and partner options. Walsh also used the briefing to argue that airport charges in India are too high, saying the market would perform much better with lower charges and taxes. Visibility on specific A350 routes will come closer to their introduction, he said.
